full_judgment:
9. Mr AJ Mohammad Ali, learned Advocate with Mr Wahiduzzman Shohel, Advocates, appearing for the defendant-appellant, submits that, learned Judge in the body of the judgment did not consider the plaint case but learned Judge considered the fault of defendant's case which is not that proper way to dispose of suit. Learned Advocate submits that it is a cardinal principle of law that plaintiff is to prove his case but learned Judge misread the depositions of witnesses and did not settle whether there was agreement or contract but there is no evidence on record to show that defendant received money from plaintiff which plaintiff failed to prove in spite of that learned Joint District Judge upon misconception of the Evidence Act wrongly shifted the onus upon the shoulder of defendant to prove that the alleged signature was not put by him and illegally decreed the suit and thereby committed error of law in decreeing the suit, as such, decree as passed was passed without considering materials on record also depositions of witnesses is liable to be set aside. 

 10. Mr Fida M Kamal with Mr Abdul Mannan, learned Advocates, appearing for the plaintiff-respondent, on the other hand, submits that, learned Judge having considered materials on record, depositions of witnesses as such, committed no illegality in decreeing the suit. Learned Advocate on reference to depositions of witnesses and also defendant's case submits that as per section 103 of the Evidence Act defendant is required to prove his case which he put by way of written statement. Learned Advocate further submits that defendant did not pay any court fee for the money which the defendant claimed from plaintiff and further submits that defendant filed number of criminal cases against plaintiff which dismissed and which therefore implied shows that there was agreement between the parties. Learned Advocate also submits that in one of the case filed by plaintiff, defendant was convicted and Criminal Appeal No. 535 of 2005 is pending for decision. Leaned Advocate further submits that when defendant denied his signature it is the duty casted upon the defendant to prove this fact but defendant did not take any initiative to examine the alleged signature by hand writing expert which proves that the signature of defendant on agreement is of him. Learned Advocate submits that judgment having passed on consideration of exhibits and depositions of the witnesses cannot be said to be a judgment passed or decision arrived on non-consideration of depositions of witnesses as such, the judgment is sustainable in law. 

 11. On the submissions of the learned Advocates of the party’s two question calls for determination, (i) whether the contract is genuine and next (ii) if it is found to be supported by evidence on record, then money transacted as claimed by plaintiff was actually received by defendant. 

 23. Taka 2,37,50,000 is a huge amount. In business such huge amount is to be transacted either by pay order or by account payee cheque, or by demand draft, rarely in cash. If it is in cash, on the event of apprehension of any breach, a document to show such payment shall have to be retained with reliable witnesses by the claimant. In the instant case it is the case of plaintiff that such huge amount was transacted in cash. From depositions of witnesses as aforesaid it appears that the witnesses make contradictory statements in between them i.e. some witnesses say money was transacted by hand and some witnesses say that money was transacted in 4 gunny bags, another says bags were tied and not opened to ascertain as whether in gunny bags Taka 2,37,50,000 were there or not. Another factum is also to be noted that such huge amount was transacted but no receipt was produced from the side of plaintiff and no endorsement was taken on the back side of the agreement. It may be true that contract is genuine and also it may be true the work order was given but in the matter of payment of money the depositions of the witnesses are very weak and does not in any manner speak such huge amount was actually received by defendant. Another factum strikes if we take the case of the plaintiff as true, then how was such a huge amount of money carried by defendant and whether such huge money was withdrawn from Bank is also misty. It is in evidence that such money was withdrawn from different Banks but no Bank documents was produced before the court to show that actually money was lifted before the signing of the agreement. 

 26. It appears that work order was issued on 4-4-2006. It is a business contract between defendant and plaintiff, but there is no evidence that such work order was received by defendant and that the defendant excepting claim of 50% of advance money as condition, out of total value, i.e. Taka 2,37,50,000 was paid but no supporting document has been produced from the side of plaintiff to prove that such money was received by defendant. From the aforesaid finding, we may summarize that the contract may be true, and work order may be made but it is very difficult to hold that the work order was sent to defendant and that the defendant received Taka 2,37,50,000 from plaintiff. We find merit in the appeal.
